A season is a distinct, recurring period of time that has a recognizable character — defined by weather, nature, an activity, or a cultural pattern. It's a "window" in the year that you can identify and name.
Meaning 1: One of the four natural divisions of the year

This is the most fundamental meaning. A year is divided into four seasons, each roughly three months long, each with its own weather and amount of daylight:

  • Spring (roughly March–May in the Northern Hemisphere): temperatures warm up, plants begin to bloom, days gradually get longer.
  • Summer (roughly June–August): the hottest period, the longest days, the most sunlight.
  • Autumn / Fall (roughly September–November): temperatures cool, leaves change colour and drop, days shorten.
  • Winter (roughly December–February): the coldest period, the shortest days, snowfall in many places.

"India experiences all four seasons, though the transitions vary by region."

Important: These months are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere. When it is summer in India (June–August), it is winter in Australia.

Also, not every part of the world has four seasons. Many tropical regions — including much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa — divide the year into just two seasons: the rainy season (or wet season) and the dry season. This is still the same word doing the same job: naming a recognizable period of the year by its dominant character.
Meaning 2: Any recurring period associated with a type of weather, event, or activity

Building on the first meaning, season is used broadly for any period of the year that has a consistent, recognizable identity — not just spring/summer/winter/autumn. These "seasons" come around regularly each year:

  • The monsoon season: the period of heavy rains.
  • The harvest season: when crops are gathered.
  • The growing season: the stretch of the year when weather allows plants to grow.
  • The tourist season (also called the high season): the time of year when a place is most visited.
  • The holiday season: the festive period around Christmas, Hanukkah, and New Year in many Western countries (roughly November–January).
  • Flu season: the time of year when influenza spreads most widely.
  • Allergy season: when pollen levels are high and allergies flare up.
  • Wedding season: the time of year when most weddings take place.

The idea is always the same: a season is a window of time that comes around again each year and has its own recognizable flavour.
Meaning 3: A period when a sport is played

In sports, a season refers to the official period during which a sport's games are scheduled and played — it has a clear beginning and end each year.

"The cricket season runs from April to September."
"The IPL season is one of the most-watched events in India."

Sporting seasons are often divided into phases:

  • Pre-season: practice matches or preparation before official play begins.
  • Regular season: the main stretch of competitive matches.
  • Post-season / playoffs: the final rounds to determine a champion.
Meaning 4: A complete run of episodes of a TV show

In modern everyday usage, season refers to a complete set of television episodes made and released together as one block.

"Have you watched Season 3 of Panchayat?"
"The show was cancelled after two seasons."

Each season typically continues the story, and is treated as its own chapter. (In British English, this is often called a series rather than a season, but both words are widely understood everywhere.)
Meaning 5: A period of performances or artistic programming

A season can refer to a scheduled period during which a theatre, opera company, orchestra, or other performing arts group presents its shows.

"The National Theatre's new season features eight productions."
"The symphony orchestra's season runs from October to May."

These two phrases are very common and important to know.

"In season" means something — most often a food — is currently available naturally, fresh, and at its best, because conditions are right for it. When a fruit or vegetable is in season, it is usually tastier, more nutritious, and cheaper, because it is grown and harvested locally at the natural time it is meant to ripen.

Mangoes are in season in India from May to July — that's when they're at their sweetest and most plentiful.
Strawberries are in season in summer.

"Out of season" means something is not naturally available right now. If you buy mangoes in December in India, they are out of season — likely imported, stored for months, or artificially produced. They may look the same but are rarely as good.

These phrases also appear in other contexts:

  • Hunting: An animal is "in season" when it is legally permitted to hunt it, and "out of season" when hunting it is prohibited by law.
  • Animals and biology: A female animal is said to be "in season" (or "in heat") when she is at the stage in her reproductive cycle when she is ready to mate.
Meaning 7: The social season (historical, but still encountered)

Historically — especially in Britain and much of Europe — the Season (often written with a capital S) referred to a specific period in late spring and summer when wealthy, aristocratic, and upper-class families would travel to cities like London to attend balls, formal dinners, horse races, and social gatherings. Young women from elite families were formally introduced to society during the Season, and it was the main arena for social networking and marriage arrangements among the upper class.

This meaning is essentially obsolete in everyday modern life, but you will encounter it in classic literature, period dramas (like Bridgerton), and discussions of social history.

These are phrases built around season that you will regularly meet:

  • High season / Peak season: The busiest, most popular time of year for a place or activity — usually tourism. Prices are typically higher. (Opposite: low season or off season.)
  • Low season / Off season: The quieter, less popular time of year. Prices tend to be lower and crowds smaller.
  • Season ticket: A single ticket that gives the holder access to all matches or all performances throughout an entire season, without buying individual tickets each time. Very common in sports and theatre.
  • Open season: Originally, the legally permitted period for hunting a specific animal. Figuratively, in everyday speech, it describes a situation where anyone can freely criticize or attack a person or group without restriction.

    "After the scandal broke, it was open season on the company's CEO."

  • The silly season: An informal British expression for the period — usually summer — when Parliament is not sitting and news is slow, so newspapers fill their pages with trivial, unusual, or lighthearted stories.
  • Season's greetings: A polite, inclusive phrase used during the December holiday period to wish someone well, without assuming which specific holiday they celebrate. You will see it on cards and decorations.
  • In good season (old-fashioned): At the right time; with enough time to spare. Rarely used today, but you may see it in older texts.

No matter which meaning you encounter, season always does the same job: it names a recurring period of time that has a distinct, recognizable identity. Whether it's one of the four natural periods of the year, the time when mangoes are at their sweetest, the stretch of months when your favourite show releases new episodes, or the period when a cricket team plays its matches — the word is always pointing to a window of time that comes around again and can be named and recognized.
